checks.name: the sort-merge join has a wall on each side
orderBy is a range wall, and runs an extra job to sample the ranges
sortWithinPartitions sorts each pile where it lies: no wall
orderBy's extra job reads the whole table to sample it: the table is read twice
SQL's UNION ALL stacks piles (no wall); plain UNION removes duplicates, and that is a wall
union stacks the two tables' piles: 4 and 4 make 8, each pile whole
coalesce(2) merges neighbouring piles where they stand: piles 1 and 2, then piles 3 and 4
a step that follows another on the same key reuses its deal: a window over each clinic, then a count per clinic, builds one wall, with or without a deal up front
a cached deal by clinic serves a later count with no new wall (Episode 17's teaser)
slow has two walls: a round-robin deal, then the hash deal the count needs
fast has one wall
kept has one wall: the count finds its rows already dealt by clinic
explain() shows slow's two Exchange lines
classic Spark, after line 5 has run: explain() prints the final plan above the starting plan, so each wall's Exchange line appears twice (slow 4, fast 2, kept 2)
over Spark Connect, explain() shows the starting plan before and after line 5 runs (slow 2, fast 1, kept 1)
cast: slow's first wall carries every row, and its second the partial counts
cast: fast's one wall carries only partial counts
cast: kept's one wall carries every row
big: slow's first wall carries every row, and its second the partial counts
big: fast's one wall carries only partial counts
big: kept's one wall carries every row
at scale, partial counts are one per clinic per pile: fast's 8 piles x 5 clinics, slow's 200 x 5
a deal up front can save a wall yet send every row: groupBy(clinic, x), then a window over clinic
at scale, fast moves the fewest bytes, then kept, then slow
